story.title: Severe Thanksgiving Storm Causes Widespread Flooding and Power Outages
story.summary: A powerful storm impacted the East Coast during Thanksgiving, resulting in significant flooding and widespread power outages. Nearly 1 million customers experienced power loss, with reports indicating that around 940,000 were affected at the peak of the outages. Cleanup efforts are underway as millions deal with the aftermath of the storm, which brought heavy rain and high winds, toppling trees and flooding streets.

event_overview.title: About Day Storm
event_overview.subject: Day Storm
event_overview.summary: “Day Storm” refers here to the Midwest-to-Eastern U.S. Thanksgiving storm of November 2026, a strong low-pressure system that developed near the Southeast coast and moved north along the East Coast during the Thanksgiving holiday. It combined heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in the East with wintry precipitation in parts of the Mid-Mississippi Valley, disrupting travel and public events.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The system developed on November 25, 2026, intensified and moved up the East Coast through Thanksgiving on November 26, and continued to produce impacts into November 27.

facts.label: Storm type and track
facts.value: The National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center characterized it as a strong coastal storm: low pressure formed off the Southeast coast and tracked northeastward along the Eastern Seaboard.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Its principal coastal hazards extended from the Carolinas into the Northeast, while associated winter weather affected parts of the Mid-Mississippi Valley, including Missouri.

facts.label: Main hazards
facts.value: Forecast and warning materials identified heavy rain, strong winds, major coastal flooding, beach erosion and some wintry precipitation as the central hazards; coastal flood warnings extended from North Carolina to southern Connecticut at the storm's peak.

facts.label: Notable public-event disruption
facts.value: In New York City, officials postponed the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thanksgiving Day to Saturday, November 28, citing expected high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major Thanksgiving-week disruptions, including the parade postponement and flooding and power-outage impacts; it does not aim to document every local forecast, warning, damage report, restoration update or travel disruption caused by the broader storm.

explore_lenses.label: Why was the coastal flooding so severe?
explore_lenses.title: Wind and high tides amplified the water rise
explore_lenses.summary: The most damaging flooding was not solely a rainfall story: strong onshore winds coincided with high-tide cycles, pushing water into coastal and bayside communities. That combination helps explain why some places saw exceptional tide levels and road inundation.

claims.text: The National Weather Service forecast that the storm's strong pressure gradient would drive storm surge, with high-tide cycles producing widespread moderate to major coastal flooding in parts of the New York metropolitan area.
ABC News reported that Cape May recorded a record 9.41-foot tide and that Atlantic City reached its highest tide since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

New Jersey's pre-storm emergency order identified coastal and bayside areas as the highest-risk locations because high tides, heavy rain and 50–70 mph gusts could make roads impassable and isolate communities.

explore_lenses.label: Why will restoring power take time?
explore_lenses.title: Wind damage created a large, uneven repair job
explore_lenses.summary: The outage count reflects widespread wind impacts across multiple utility territories, rather than a single failure. Restoration can vary substantially by location when crews must first address downed trees, damaged lines and unsafe travel conditions.

claims.text: ABC News reported winds of 50 to 70 mph from North Carolina to Massachusetts, which toppled trees, brought down power lines and damaged property; nearly half a million households remained without power Friday afternoon.

Before the storm, the National Weather Service's Mount Holly office warned that widespread tree damage and power outages were likely, especially near the coast and across Delmarva, where forecast gusts reached 60–70 mph in places.

New Jersey's emergency declaration authorized statewide coordination with county and municipal emergency management, state agencies, volunteer organizations and private-sector partners, as well as road closures, shelters and National Guard activation if needed.

explore_lenses.label: What hazards remain after the storm?
explore_lenses.title: Residual flooding first, then another rain system
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate threat was easing on November 27, but residual coastal flooding and beach erosion remained possible around high tide. Forecasters also expected a separate, less consequential rain event late Sunday into early Monday.

claims.text: Forecast: The National Weather Service New York office said residual coastal flooding remained possible on the south shore and minor flooding was likely around western Long Island Sound high tide on November 27; beach flooding and dune erosion could continue into the afternoon.

Forecast: The same NWS office expected rain Sunday night into early Monday, estimating around a half-inch of rain and stating that hydrologic impacts were not anticipated, although gusty winds and marine conditions could increase.
Forecast: NWS aviation guidance said rain was likely after midnight Sunday into early Monday around the New York metro, with lower flight conditions possible before improvement later Monday.

story_report.summary: A Thanksgiving storm brought heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding across the East Coast, disrupting travel and leaving large numbers of customers without electricity. Power outages peaked at about 940,000 customers, while 375,000 were still without service in the supplied outage snapshot. Winds of 50 to 70 mph from North Carolina to Massachusetts toppled trees, downed power lines and damaged property as communities began cleanup.

sections.heading: Coastal flooding hits New Jersey
sections.body: The storm’s pressure gradient and high-tide cycles were forecast to produce widespread moderate to major coastal flooding in parts of the New York metropolitan area. Cape May recorded a record 9.41-foot tide, while Atlantic City reached its highest tide since Superstorm Sandy in 2012, ABC News reported. Before the storm, New Jersey identified coastal and bayside communities as particularly vulnerable because high tides, heavy rain and 50-to-70-mph gusts could make roads impassable and isolate residents.

sections.heading: Restoration and emergency coordination
sections.body: The National Weather Service had warned that coastal areas and the Delmarva region could see widespread tree damage and outages, with gusts of 60 to 70 mph in some locations. New Jersey’s emergency declaration authorized coordination among state and local emergency managers, agencies, volunteer groups and private-sector partners, including potential road closures, shelters and National Guard activation. Nearly half a million households remained without power Friday afternoon, according to ABC News.

sections.heading: Additional rain remains forecast
sections.body: The National Weather Service’s New York office said residual coastal flooding remained possible along the south shore, with minor flooding likely near western Long Island Sound at high tide on November 27. Beach flooding and dune erosion could continue into the afternoon. The office also forecast rain Sunday night into early Monday, with about a half-inch expected and no hydrologic impacts anticipated, though gusty winds, marine conditions and lower flight conditions could increase.

related_stories.title: Cleanup Efforts Underway After Thanksgiving Storm Disrupts East Coast
related_stories.summary: A Thanksgiving storm has caused significant disruptions across the East Coast, leaving approximately 480,000 homes and businesses without power as of Friday, down from 900,000 the previous day. The storm brought heavy rain and strong winds, leading to travel delays and necessitating water rescues from New York to Virginia. While conditions are improving, some areas remain on alert for potential high-tide flooding.

related_stories.title: Kenyan cult leader convicted of manslaughter for 123 deaths, adding to previous murder sentences
related_stories.summary: Paul Mackenzie, the leader of a starvation cult in Kenya, has been found guilty of manslaughter for the deaths of 123 followers. This conviction follows his earlier sentencing to 200 years in prison for the murder of nearly 200 children. Mackenzie has also faced charges related to radicalization and organized criminal activity.

related_stories.title: Allies Condemn Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia, Pledge Support
related_stories.summary: Officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye have condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, labeling them as 'heinous.' During discussions in Islamabad, the three nations reaffirmed their commitment to protect Saudi Arabia's security under a defense pact. This collaboration aims to bolster regional stability amid ongoing threats.

related_stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada Upholds Quebec's Ban on Religious Symbols for Public Servants
related_stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has largely upheld Quebec's Bill 21, which prohibits public servants from wearing religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans, and crosses. The law, enacted in 2019, aims to maintain a secular state, but has faced criticism for potentially infringing on individual rights. Legal challenges were brought forth by various groups, including teachers from different religious backgrounds, who argued that the law violates their fundamental rights.
